Summary: Father emailed a proposed temporary January parenting schedule, based on Mother's work schedule, with a response deadline of January 5.
Full Message: Subject: Proposed January Parenting Schedule (Temporary) | To reduce confusion and avoid conflict while we are waiting for mediation and court orders, I am proposing the attached parenting schedule for January only. This proposal is temporary and without prejudice, and does not replace the parenting plan I filed with the court on November 14, 2025. I prepared this schedule in the best interests of the children and took into account the work schedule you provided. Days labeled 'Mom/Dad' indicate a morning transition with Mom and an evening transition with Dad, and vice versa. Weekday transitions will occur at school dismissal. Weekend and MLK Day transitions will occur at 9:00 a.m. if you are not working later that day, or at 5:30 p.m. if you are working. If you agree, or if you have specific conflicts with this schedule, please let me know by January 5, 2026, so they can be addressed in advance. My goal is to provide the children with a clear and consistent schedule so they are not left confused. [proposed schedule attached]
Impact: Father's proactive proposal established a written record of his effort to create structure and predictability for the children during a period without a court-ordered schedule. The imposed response deadline of January 5 created a reasonable window for resolution before the schedule took effect, reducing the risk of last-minute confusion for the children.

Summary: Mother declined Father's proposed January schedule, stated children were capable of reading her work schedule themselves, and proposed continuing the existing arrangement where children stay with her when she is not working.
Full Message: Subject: Proposed January Parenting Schedule (Temporary) | I agree with your proposal of streamlining the times to 9am and 5:30pm for non school days, as well as transitioning after school on school days. I have previously proposed this in my email on November 5th. I do not agree with your proposed plan for January. I have tried to be flexible with the kids remaining with you if there were interrupted work days on my schedule in return for time with them on another day but I have been met with resistance on your behalf. Therefore I think we should continue with the way we have always done it until mediation and that would mean, the kids are with me when I'm not working. They also have a copy of my schedule and are very capable of reading that schedule to know where they're going on any given day. Thank you for your proposal. Kind regards, Jennifer
Impact: Mother's rejection of a structured schedule in favor of a work-schedule-driven arrangement maintained ambiguity about the children's custody placement on any given day. Mother's statement that the children are capable of reading her schedule and determining their own whereabouts placed logistical and scheduling responsibility directly on the children rather than on the parents.

Summary: Father acknowledged Mother's rejection of the January schedule proposal, noted the absence of any counter-proposal to his court-filed parenting plan, and stated he would temporarily follow Mother's preferred arrangement without agreement or waiver of concerns.
Full Message: Subject: Proposed January Parenting Schedule (Temporary) | Understood. I filed a proposed parenting plan with the court nearly two months ago and, to date, have not received any response or alternative proposal. I suggested a temporary January schedule based on the children's best interests and your provided work schedule, with the goal of providing consistency and predictability. You declined and have instead insisted on an approach determined solely by your preferences, continuing to demonstrate an unwillingness to work cooperatively or be flexible. To avoid further conflict, I will temporarily follow your indicated schedule, but I do so without agreement or waiver of my previously stated concerns regarding structure, communication, and the children's involvement. If you are open to discussing a more collaborative and structured approach in the future that is centered around the children's best interest, I remain open for discussion.
Impact: Father's written response documented his accommodation of Mother's preferred arrangement while preserving his objections on the record. The notation that Mother's approach was determined solely by her preferences, without reference to the children's need for structure, established a documented basis for the ongoing scheduling conflict.

Summary: Father emailed Mother a request to limit non-urgent communications to daytime hours between 7:00 AM and 7:00 PM. No reply was ever received.
Full Message: Subject: Communication Parameters | Please direct non-urgent communications to reasonable daytime hours, defined as 7:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m., or another mutually agreed timeframe. Communications outside of these hours should be limited to urgent or emergency matters only. This request is made to ensure orderly, predictable, and appropriate parent-to-parent communication. Thank you for your cooperation. [NO REPLY EVER RECEIVED]
Impact: Father's request to establish communication boundaries received no response, leaving co-parenting communication protocols undefined and unenforceable. Mother's failure to acknowledge or reply to the request continued a pattern of non-engagement with structured co-parenting efforts.

Summary: Father proposed that February parenting time follow the schedule from his November 14 court-filed parenting plan, adjusted for February dates and his previously noticed February unavailability.
Full Message: Subject: Proposed February Parenting Schedule | Hello, To provide clarity and predictability for February, I am proposing that we follow the temporary parenting schedule set forth in the parenting plan I filed with the court on November 14, 2025, adjusted for February calendar dates and my previous notice of unavailability that I sent you on December 15 for the dates from February 21 through February 27, 2026. Having a schedule in place ahead of time would help avoid last-minute changes and make things easier for the kids. If you'd like to handle February differently, feel free to share what you have in mind. Mathew
Impact: Father proactively proposed a structured February schedule with adequate advance notice, reducing the likelihood of last-minute schedule disputes. Father's reference to his court-filed parenting plan reinforced the existence of a documented formal proposal that had not been addressed by Mother.

Summary: Mother submitted a proposed February schedule using Mom/Dad notation, with transitions occurring after school, and proposed an extra overnight at Father's on February 7 to avoid a single-day back-and-forth.
Full Message: Subject: Proposed February Parenting Schedule | Here is my proposal: M stands for mom, D stands for dad. Swaps will happen on the proposed day after school. M: 1/29 / D: 2/4 / M: 2/11 (this allows an additional day at dad's house to minimize back and forth for one day on Feb. 7th) / D: 2/17 / M: 2/19 through February vacation
Impact: Mother provided a February schedule proposal without addressing Father's November 14 court-filed parenting plan or their son's birthday, leaving key matters unresolved. The proposal did not account for Father's previously noticed February unavailability, creating a gap in coverage for the children during that period.

Summary: Father reviewed Mother's February proposal, noted it did not address the court-filed parenting plan or their son's birthday, and stated he would follow Mother's schedule without agreement or waiver of objections.
Full Message: Subject: Proposed February Parenting Schedule | I have reviewed your proposed February schedule. The proposal does not address the temporary parenting plan I filed or our son's birthday. I do not see a productive path to agreement by email. To avoid further back-and-forth, I will follow the February schedule you outlined, without agreement and without waiver of my objections. Mathew
Impact: Mother's proposed February schedule omitted their son's birthday, excluding Father from participating in advance planning for a significant family date. Father's written objection preserved the record of these gaps while preventing further unproductive exchange.

Summary: Father provided advance written notice that he would be out of state and unavailable from March 21 through March 26, 2026.
Full Message: Subject: Dates of Unavailability - March 21-26 | For planning and childcare purposes, I am providing advance notice that I will be out of state and unavailable from March 21 through March 26, 2026.
Impact: Father's advance notice allowed sufficient time for the parties to plan appropriate childcare and parenting coverage during his absence. The written notice established a documented record of the dates and the purpose of the notification.

Summary: Mother acknowledged receipt of Father's unavailability notice with a brief reply.
Full Message: Subject: Dates of Unavailability - March 21-26 | Received. Sent from my iPhone
Impact: Mother's one-word acknowledgment confirmed receipt but provided no indication of how she intended to address the children's care during Father's absence. The absence of any follow-up proposal left coverage for that period unresolved.

Summary: Father moved Mother's text-based March/April schedule proposal to email, analyzed the overnight distribution, rejected the proposal as inequitable, and submitted his own equal-time counter-proposal.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | I'm moving your recommended March/April schedule to email for clarity. Below is what you sent: [4:17 PM text]: My recommendation is you get the kids March 1 at 5:30pm or whatever time Mathew gets out of work. I get them back 3/5 after school. Back to you after school 3/9. My house after school 3/12. Your house after school 3/19 until 3/26 I get them back after school. You're house after school 4/1, my house after school 4/3. You get them back after school 4/7. My house after school 4/10. They come back to you 4/12 in the afternoon and back to me 4/15 after school. You're house 4/20 after school and my house 4/23 after school. [8:30 PM text]: Nevermind the end of March. I know you'll be away 3/21-3/26. After placing the proposed dates into calendar format (reflecting your 8:30 PM revision removing March 21-26), the allocation results in 41 overnights with you and 20 overnights with me during this period. It provides only one instance over this two-month period in which I would have more than three consecutive overnights. The proposal assigns parenting time on dates that correspond with your work schedule. I do not agree to this proposal. Attached is my proposed March/April schedule, which reflects a substantially equal allocation of parenting time and a consistent structure. [ATTACHED PROPOSED SCHEDULE FROM FATHER]
Impact: Mother's proposed March/April schedule, if adopted, would have resulted in Father receiving fewer than half the overnights during the two-month period, representing a significant imbalance in parenting time. Father's analysis and documented counter-proposal established a written record of the disparity and his effort to negotiate toward equal time.

Summary: Father responded to Mother's request for additional April time by noting that his proposal already achieved equal overnights across the two months and asked her to identify specific dates so parity could be maintained.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | Regarding your request for additional April time, my proposal was structured to provide equal overnights across March and April overall. If you're requesting an adjustment to April overnights, please identify the specific dates so we can review corresponding March dates to maintain overall parity.
Impact: Father's structured response to Mother's April request maintained the framework of equal parenting time and required specificity before any adjustment could be evaluated. Prevented an open-ended expansion of Mother's parenting time without a corresponding offset.

Summary: Mother identified specific April dates she wanted and characterized Father's planned March absence as a choice that resulted in fewer overnights for him, while noting she accepted certain March dates favorable to Father despite not working those nights.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | I want them April 15th after school through the weekend and April 23rd after school though the weekend. It is your choice to go away in March, which results in you getting less over nights, and I'm fine with your proposal for March where you get to keep them from 3/16 after school till 3/20 even though I'm not working. And I'm also ok with you getting them back a day early on 3/31 to make up for some of the lost over nights due to you being away. Sent from my iPhone
Impact: Mother's framing of Father's planned absence as a personal choice used to justify reduced parenting time sought to shift the basis for schedule allocation away from equal division. Presenting concessions as generosity rather than as part of an equitable framework introduced a dynamic that could pressure Father into accepting fewer overnights.

Summary: Father informed Mother he was away and would review and respond to her counter-proposal upon his return.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | I'm away and will review and respond when I return.
Impact: Father's brief notice provided Mother with a documented explanation for any delay in response. Established a clear record that Father had received the message and would respond, preventing a claim of non-response.

Summary: Father responded to Mother's April request, analyzing the overnight imbalance created by her proposal, noting her own unavailability exceeded his, and requesting that she specify exact dates and corresponding March adjustments.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | My March unavailability was provided with advance notice and was incorporated into a proposed schedule that equalizes total overnights across March and April combined. For context, your periods of unavailability in both March and April exceed mine. My proposal accounts for both parents' schedules and still results in substantially equal parenting time over the two-month period. Your requested April adjustments increase your overnights without corresponding March adjustments, creating an imbalance. My six days of unavailability in March do not warrant a structural shift in overall parenting time, just as your 12 days of unavailability in March do not. If you are requesting April 15 and April 23 weekends, specify the exact start and end dates and exchange times so the proposal is clear. Please also identify which March dates you propose to adjust so that overall balance is maintained.
Impact: Father's documented analysis of overnight distribution provided a factual basis for rejecting Mother's April request and established that Mother's own work schedule resulted in greater unavailability than Father's planned absence. Required Mother to present a specific and balanced counter-proposal rather than expanding her parenting time unilaterally.

Summary: Mother confirmed agreement with Father's March schedule and reiterated specific April requests including keeping the children through April 29 during school vacation week, while objecting to the characterization of her work schedule as unavailability.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | As outlined in my email dated February 20, I am in agreement with your proposed schedule for March, which provides you with five additional overnights—March 2, 16, 17, 18, and 31—despite of me being off those nights. With respect to April 15, as previously stated, I request that the children return to my care after school on that date. They will then return to your care after school on Monday, April 20. On April 23, the children will return to my care after school. The following week is the children's school vacation week. I am requesting to keep the children through Wednesday, April 29, in order to spend meaningful time with them during their school break. Although my work schedule for that week will not open for shift requests or self-scheduling until early April, it is my intention to schedule my shifts toward the end of that week so that I may have consecutive days off to spend with the children. I would also like to clarify that I have not claimed to be unavailable at any time during March or April. My scheduled work nights do not constitute unavailability. In the event of a need or emergency, I remain available and prepared to be present for the children. To the extent my work nights are being characterized as unavailability, that is inaccurate. Historically, my work schedule has only been used as general guidance in determining how parenting time has been allocated between us. Sent from my iPhone
Impact: Mother's confirmation of March agreement moved one portion of the schedule forward while leaving April unresolved, prolonging uncertainty about the children's schedule for the spring period. Mother's position that her work nights do not constitute unavailability, while simultaneously using them as the basis for parenting time allocation, introduced an inconsistency in the framework being applied.

Summary: Father confirmed March was settled and expressed agreement to Mother's requested April 23–29 dates as consistent with equal overall allocation, and requested Mother's confirmation so a final schedule could be issued.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | Great, March is confirmed then. I am agreeable to April 23-29, which maintains equal overall allocation over March/April. Any other adjustments would create an imbalance. Please confirm that you agree to the above schedule reflecting equal parenting time and I'll update the schedules and send them back.
Impact: Father's written confirmation of March and conditional agreement to April 23–29 advanced the scheduling process while preserving equal-time parameters. The request for Mother's written confirmation was necessary to finalize the children's schedule and prevent future disputes about what had been agreed.

Summary: Father followed up after ten days without a reply to his March 3 email, quoted Mother's own prior request for written confirmation, and stated he would proceed under his proposed April schedule absent a specific counter-proposal.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | 'To avoid future misunderstandings, I am requesting that we confirm the March and April parenting schedule in writing. Please either confirm your agreement with the previously proposed schedule or provide any revisions you would like to suggest. A timely response would be appreciated so that expectations are clear for everyone involved.' It has been 10 days since my March 3 email and I have not received a reply or confirmation. Unless you propose specific adjustments to maintain parity, I will proceed under the April schedule I sent.
Impact: Mother's ten-day failure to respond to a written confirmation request left the children's April schedule unconfirmed and created ongoing uncertainty about their custody arrangements. Father's follow-up documented the delay and established that he would proceed with his proposed schedule in the absence of a timely response.

Summary: Mother confirmed she agreed to Father's April proposal with her adjustment of April 23–29.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | I'm ok with your proposal for April with my adjustment of 4/23-4/29. Sent from my iPhone
Impact: Mother's belated confirmation came only after Father's follow-up, reflecting a pattern of requiring escalation before scheduling matters are resolved. The brief reply left the precise end date of the April 23–29 period unspecified, creating ambiguity requiring further clarification.

Summary: Father confirmed April was set and attached the finalized schedule, noting ambiguity about whether Mother's period ended April 29 or April 30 and asking for clarification.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | Great, April is set and attached. I was unsure as to whether 'through April 29' meant ending on April 29 or ending April 30. The attached reflects ending April 29. If you meant ending April 30, let me know and I will update the schedule.
Impact: Ambiguity in Mother's prior confirmation required Father to seek clarification on a basic end date, prolonging the schedule finalization process. Father's proactive follow-up prevented a potential dispute about the exchange date at the end of the vacation period.

Summary: Mother clarified that she intended the April period to end April 30.
Full Message: Subject: March–April Parenting Schedule | I meant ending April 30th. Thank you
Impact: Mother's clarification resolved the ambiguity about the April end date but required an additional exchange to finalize a detail that should have been specified in her original confirmation. Extended the scheduling negotiation by one additional round.
